h1: Homebrewing on a budget with kitchen kit you already own
title: Homebrewing With Kitchen Kit You Own | Craft Beer School
desc: What kitchen kit you can brew with, the few things you must buy and how to brew a first small batch of beer at home on a tight budget in India.
teaser: Your kitchen already holds most of a brewery. Here is what to use and the three things you must buy.
standfirst: You do not need a shiny starter kit to brew your first beer. A stockpot, a sieve and a clean bucket go a long way. We go through what you can borrow from the kitchen and what you really have to buy.
sections: Most of a brewery is already in your kitchen

Brewing beer comes down to a few jobs: soak grain in hot water, boil the sweet liquid with hops, cool it, add yeast and keep it clean while it ferments. Most of those jobs need nothing more than kitchen kit.

Start small. A 5 litre batch fits in the pots most Indian kitchens already have and makes about fifteen 330 ml bottles. That is enough to learn on and small enough that a mistake costs little. Our guide to small batch brewing explains why small batches teach faster.

• A big pot: a 10 litre steel or aluminium stockpot is enough for a 5 litre batch. A large pressure cooker body works as a pot with the lid off; never brew under pressure.
  • A thin cotton cloth or voile bag: to hold crushed grain in the pot, the brew in a bag method on a small scale.
  • A sieve and a ladle: for moving hot wort and catching hops.
  • Kitchen scales: grams matter for hops and priming sugar.
  • A measuring jug: for water volumes.
  • A big steel bowl or sink: for an ice bath to cool the pot.

On an induction stove, check the pot's base with a magnet first. Our guide to brewing on an induction stove covers the details.
The three things you must buy

Some jobs the kitchen cannot do well. Spend your money here:

  1. A food grade fermenter with an airlock. A food grade bucket with a lid and a grommet for an airlock is cheap. Do not use a paint bucket or anything that held chemicals. A 10 litre bucket suits a 5 litre batch with room for foam.
  2. A hydrometer and trial jar. It measures gravity, which tells you how much sugar you have and when fermentation is finished. Without it you are guessing when to bottle, which is how bottles explode.
  3. A no-rinse sanitiser. Kitchen soap cleans but does not sanitise. Soap residue also kills beer foam. A brewing sanitiser is the cheapest insurance you will buy.

A digital kitchen probe thermometer is fine for a first brew. Check it in ice water, where it should read 0 °C. The mash, where grain soaks in hot water, needs to sit between about 64 and 68 °C for an hour for enzymes to turn starch into sugar. On a small stove, a towel wrapped round the pot or a spell in a warm oven that has been switched off holds the heat well enough.

If all-grain feels like too much for a first try, a batch using malt extract skips the mash entirely. It costs a little more per litre but needs even less kit.
Keeping fermentation cool on a budget

Temperature is where a budget brew usually fails in India. Ale yeast prefers about 18 to 22 °C. Fermentation itself warms the beer above the room. A fermenter left in a 30 °C room can run several degrees hotter inside, which gives harsh, fruity and solvent flavours.

The cheapest fix is a water bath. Stand the fermenter in a bucket of water and swap in frozen water bottles twice a day. Draping a wet towel over it adds a little evaporative cooling. A heat-tolerant yeast such as kveik is the other route: many strains ferment cleanly at 30 °C and above.
Bottles and caps without a shop bill

Save bottles. Brown glass beer bottles that take a crown cap are ideal; avoid twist-off necks, because crown caps do not seal on them. Rinse each bottle straight after it is emptied. A bench capper and a bag of crown caps are a small spend. Swing-top bottles need no capper at all if you can collect them.
What a budget brew cannot teach you

Hops and grain are the other spend. A small batch keeps that low. A 5 litre pale ale needs only about 1 to 1.2 kg of crushed pale malt, 15 to 25 grams of hops and part of a sachet of dry yeast. Buy crushed malt in small packs and brew within a couple of weeks, because crushed grain goes stale quickly in humid weather.

A kitchen brew will teach you the sequence and the feel of brewing. It will not tell you why your beer tastes thin, why it turned sour or why the next one came out different. That needs an understanding of mashing, yeast and fermentation that kit cannot supply. Our guide to the homebrewing starter kit in India lists what to add once you know you are hooked.

Your first step: put your biggest pot, a sieve, a jug and your kitchen scales on the counter, then order a food grade fermenter, a hydrometer and sanitiser.
faqs: Can I brew beer with normal kitchen equipment?
Mostly yes. A stockpot, sieve, ladle, jug and scales cover the hot side. You still need a food grade fermenter with an airlock, a hydrometer and a brewing sanitiser.
Is an aluminium pot safe for brewing?
Yes, aluminium pots are fine for mashing and boiling. Do not clean them with caustic cleaners. They also do not work on induction.
How do I keep fermentation cool in an Indian summer?
Stand the fermenter in a bucket of water and add frozen bottles twice a day, or use a heat-tolerant yeast such as kveik.
